speechtext: I know that all of this refers to the Bill, but I would ask Hon. Members to delay their questions and comments until the Hon. Member finishes his debate.

Mr. Speaker, I was only taking my cue from the presentation given by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre who, in his fashion, forgot a few pertinent facts. I thought that the House would probably want to understand those facts and to have them on the record as to how things are financed and how that relates back to finances. I am sure that the Hon. Member is not enjoying my exposition. Other Members of the House certainly are because they are always prepared to be educated.
With respect to the Bill, I think that the Manitoba case is a good example as to why this Bill should be opposed. There is an underlying undercurrent of tax revolt going on in the country. People are getting fed up with the Government in Ottawa, as they were with the Government in Manitoba, imposing personal taxes on them, putting taxes on their snack foods, watching television and driving a car. Those are not luxuries. We are not talking about something that is a frivolous exercise of activity. We are talking about something that is part and parcel of everyday life.
Who is suffering most as a result of these excise taxes? If we consider one group in the community, and there are many, who suffers the most? It is older people who rely on their telephones and their television. There are probably many Members in the House who have a high percentage of senior citizens in their ridings, as I do. If one visits the apartment blocks in which they live, one will see that many of them are confined during winter months. One of the joys they are able to exercise is the picking up of the telephone to call a relative,
a son or a daughter in another city. Television is also very important in terms of a means of communication.
What do we do? We put a tax on those items. In fact, the imposition of taxes on consumption has been the highest level rise of any form of taxation in the last three years when compared to corporate taxes or income taxes. We have placed more taxes, regressive taxes, on people's ordinary necessary consumption than on any other level.
I believe that the increase has been over 70 per cent since the Government came to power. Let us consider what those taxes have been on. They have been on gasoline, snack foods, cablevision and paint. That is not tax reform. That is not a regime of receiving revenue that applies taxes according to the ability to pay or according to lifestyle.
If there is any clear indication of the distortion and bias in our tax system, it is this very Bill we are debating today. It shows how a burden is being put on those least able to bear it. Rather than trying to achieve a system of fairness and equity that would balance the need of revenue on the ability to pay, we seem to be reversing that formula. We seem to be working at it in opposite and contradictory style.
I hope that members of the Government will understand why there are such concerns. When this excise sales tax is laid on top of those being imposed at the provincial level, and increasingly at the municipal level, the levies against those least able to pay become heavier and heavier while many of those who can afford it are being let go. We are reducing the rate for them. An excise tax on cablevision may not count to the family or individual earning $50,000, $60,000 or $100,000 per year. It certainly counts for a senior citizen whose disposable income may be $20 or $30 per month. I think you know that, Mr. Speaker. You have people like that in your own riding. I do not understand this.
If there is to be true tax reform, then one may want to look clearly at this Bill as being the wrong example to follow. As I read it, the Government intends not just to follow it but to expand upon it, to broaden it, to enhance it and to enlarge it so that we will have a much broader base of consumption tax. Then, the Government will try to sell it by saying; "We will offer a tax credit to relieve some of the burden of those on lower incomes."
One need only look at the level which applies here. The threshold is $16,000. That is below the poverty line for a family in our cities across Canada. At least we put the threshold at $22,000 on the child care issue. That is the problem with using the tax credit method. It is that it becomes subject to this type of niggardly approach. The Ministers of Finance, if they are short a little revenue, can always bring the threshold down and say; "We are helping those on lowest incomes". They are not helping the working poor, or even working people themselves. All they are doing is restricting their access to some very basic necessities.
April 14, 1988

I think one of the most pernicious parts of this Bill is the one that incorporates the tax change that was brought about in this spring's Budget. There is a very important story to be told. We have been told that the trade agreement, this great economic bonanza, is nothing but good-jobs, growth and productivity. We know that that has been disputed. The report of the Department of Finance and the Economic Council of Canada mentioned less than one half of one per cent growth per year, perhaps 20,000 jobs per year, which is marginal in terms of the over-all macro-economic scale. What we are now finding out is that we will have to pay increased taxes because of that proposed trade agreement. Not only does it not deliver the bonanza that has been promised, but we will have to pay more. If one looks at the calculations of the Council and the Conference Board, we are talking about an additional $2 billion annual taxes when the trade agreement, if it ever comes into effect, would finally be fully implemented.
How does the Government of Canada intend to make up the $2 billion? Here is evidence case number one. It will increase the tax on gasoline by one cent per litre. That is a beginning. It will raise $450 million. It is not coincidental that in the financial papers accompanying the Budget there were two lines which stated: "revenue loss because of trade agreement 400 some odd million dollars", while the other states revenue gained from additional gasoline tax 400 some odd million dollars. It is a clear replacement tax for the revenue that we are losing. It is being placed on people who drive cars. We know that in a country such as Canada with our climate and geography that driving a car is not a luxury, it is a necessity. The tax falls heaviest on those who can least afford to drive.
I come back to my friends in the NDP. Why are they being defeated? Because they raised the Autopac premiums. They put another tax on that particular service. The people who really got mad are those who are driving a 1972 Chev or something and all of a sudden their Autopac premiums go up 300 per cent.
Like mine.

The Hon. Member would be mad too, I say to the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway. He would even vote against the NDP in Manitoba if he lived there.
The fact of the matter is that this is a tax that falls upon those least able to bear the burden. If we have to make up or replace not $400 million but $2 billion, and we see how the Government approaches the problem, it will not provide extra taxation for all those big corporations which are out humping for free trade, but put it on the people who do not want it. It is putting a tax on those who are carrying the burden. It is a free ride for the free trade advocates, but a very heavy load for those working people who cannot afford it. That is why this Bill has a pernicious element to it.
Let us say for the sake of argument that the full $2 billion deficit will have to be made up by increasing the tax on
Excise Tax Act
gasoline. That will mean an extra couple of dollars to fill up a tank. If it does not come from there, where will it come from? From the television set? From the telephone system? That is the real problem, and that is one of the stories that Canadians better understand: there is no free ride with free trade. Canadians will have to pay through the nose, or in this case pay through their telephone set or at the gasoline pump.
That is why this is a very important Bill. It clearly demonstrates the type of financial and economic shenanigans that we are getting ourselves into because of this trade agreement, and the type of losses that we will suffer that will have to be made up through heavier burdens of taxation, probably on consumers, because that appears to be the favourite choice and mode of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The Minister of Finance may not be around long enough to carry through on that threat. I am sure that he will not be. What we are debating today is one of the reasons why he will not have the chance to carry through on this particular formula that he has introduced in this Bill.
What we see today in Manitoba, the disillusionment and tax revolt that is going on by ordinary people who say that they have had enough, is happening right across the country. They are not fooled by the tax reform fable that has been spilled out in the country. I know for sure that Canadians see through that in spades.
That's right in Ontario.
It may be. I think that there is a real lesson here for all Governments, and I do not care of what stripe. The Hon. Member's colleagues in Manitoba are finding out in the most disastrous manner.
Yes. They are trying to raise taxes with a $600 million surplus.

Well, they did. I am sorry, the Hon. Member does not know what he is talking about. They did raise taxes.
Many ordinary people are saying that they have had enough. If we are going to fire this Government, we had better find a more equitable way of doing it than putting a tax on the basic necessities that Canadians consume.
That is why this Bill is an awful lot more important for Canadians than just the revenue it raises. It stands as a clear lesson and example of what is wrong with our tax system under the present regime, and it provides them with a very clear symbol as to why they are mad, indignant, and turning against so many of the proposals that too many Governments are attempting to get away with.

I do not wish to get into the Manitoba election, since I am not from Manitoba, but the Hon. Member from Manitoba did mention that. I want to point out to him that I am from British Columbia and last week I renewed my auto insurance. Previously it cost me approximately $400 and

last week it cost me $561. Auto insurance is increasing all over the country. No one likes that, but it is a fact. I know the Hon. Member likes to put it into Manitoba and pretend that it is only Manitobans who are suffering this, but I wish to tell the Hon. Member out of personal experience that I had to pay last week.
I also would like to note that in B.C. the conservative Government has cut our social services terribly, and taxed us too. The Pawley Government never cut back social services, as far as I could see as someone from outside of Manitoba. That province had pretty good employment with low unemployment rates through a difficult period. It was about half the rate of British Columbia. I also see a Premier who was pretty honest and took full responsibility for the defeat of his Government. From an outsider's point of view, Manitoba does not look all that bad.
I am confused about the Campeau matter. The Hon. Member said that Campeau was going to a dinner of Polish waiters-not polls-Polish. The Hon. Member was also talking about Gallup polls, and so on. I understand that was the dinner for Mr. Trudeau. I wish to ask the Hon. Member if he went to that dinner along with Mr. Campeau, and whether he agrees with the very serious remarks made by Mr. Campeau which seem to be in contradiction of his speech. I understand that Mr. Campeau, a very prominent Liberal, received many favours and many contracts from the Government of which the Hon. Member who just spoke was a member. This man is against medicare. Is that the position of the Liberal Party that the Hon. Member from Winnipeg represents?

First, I do not know what dinner Mr. Campeau attended. I was only using it as a turn of phrase that he went to a dinner for Mr. Trudeau. He may have. I was not there. I do not know if Mr. Campeau was there. I do not follow his social agenda, and I do not know which dinner he attended.
I can tell the Hon. Member, without any reservation, that I do not like what Mr. Campeau said either. I think that it was despicable. The statements made by Mr. Campeau about the blessings of another system after he has enjoyed this one is one that many of us regret, and I share with the Hon. Member a sense of indignation for the ingratitude of a man like Mr. Campeau who was given opportunity in this country.
I may have a different philosophy from the Hon. Member. I do not in any way bring down someone because they have made good. Someone who has succeeded and done well, built up a business or an enterprise deserves some credit and respect. But at the same time I think that they should also acknowledge that along the way they were able to enjoy many benefits in this country. I agree with the Hon. Member that Mr. Campeau ignoring his recent history brings shame to him and deserves the calumny that has been expressed by so many in this country, and I have no argument with that.
While we are not here to debate provincial politics, I wish to say to the Hon. Member that I do sympathize with the burden he bears of being a citizen of a province governed by the present Premier. As I have often stated, I think he took his experience in Fantasyland too seriously and is now trying to apply it to Government.
I was struck by the Hon. Member's description of the increase in his auto premiums. If I am not mistaken, he said that it went from $400 to $561. My auto insurance went from $400 to $700. Perhaps it is just that extra bit of difference in Manitoba that is the reason why Mr. Pawley is now going to lose his seat and every other seat in the province along the way.
I am not trying to make the case, and I am sure the Hon. Member knows, that Governments do not have a right to tax or to provide services. I strongly believe in that. But I am saying that there are serious problems in this country that the burden of taxation is falling on the wrong people, and that too many Governments, federal and provincial, are trying to put it at the consumption level and ignore other areas which are far more effective.
Clearly, the tax revolt going on in Manitoba is an indication. I would only ask the Hon. Member to consider the following. I also admire Mr. Pawley as being an honest man, but I do not think that his Government became very good in its second term. I think it lost its way in the second term. It started cutting back on social services, education, and other programs of that type. That became a problem for that Government, and as a result it lost the support of people who are prepared to be taxed if they receive value for it. But they do not wish to be taxed to blow a bunch of money on a telephone enterprise in Saudi Arabia, which is what the Manitoba Governments was doing, or blow money on mega projects rather than investing it in higher education or training.

Mr. Speaker, my motion today deals with a very important issue, that of direct participation of Canadians in the democratic process.
As we all know, there is no provision in Canada or in the provinces to have binding referendums on Governments. As we move into the 21st century it is extremely important that people be consulted. Therefore I have presented this motion to the House.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, a Private Member's Motion can be voted upon only if it is not talked out. I am looking at the clock; if nobody is talking one minute before six o'clock, the motion can be voted upon. I hope for the sake of democracy that those present in the House will abide by the wishes of their constituents so that the Private Member's Motion can be voted upon.
I will read my motion. It indicates:
WHEREAS the Constitution Act, 1867 provides in section 17 that there shall be one Parliament for Canada, consisting of the Queen, an Upper House styled the Senate, and the House of Commons;
AND WHEREAS it is expedient that the electors of Canada be more directly involved in the legislative process;
AND WHEREAS an initiative and referendum process is an appropriate mechanism for the determination of questions of national interest;
AND WHEREAS the Parliament of Canada should be bound to enact any measures necessary to implement decisions of the electors of Canada on questions put to them by referendum;
NOW, THEREFORE, the House of Commons resolves that an amendment to the Constitution of Canada be authorized to be made by proclamation issued by Her Excellency the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada in accordance with the schedule hereto.
I will read the schedule because it is important to note the mechanisms of a referendum and it needs an amendment to the Constitution:
1. The Constitution Act, 1867 is amended by inserting, immediately after section 19 thereof, the following section:

April 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
"20. (1) A referendum on any matter coming within the classes of subjects enumerated in section 91 may be initiated by proclamation of the Government of Canada or by petition of not less than twenty per cent of the electors of Canada addressed to the House of Commons.
(2)	A decision of the electors of Canada in a referendum held pursuant to this section is binding on the Government and the Parliament of Canada and shall, within a reasonable time after the holding of the referendum, be implemented by them in a manner consistent with their powers and authority.
(3)	No referendum shall be held on a question that is substantially the same as a question on which a referendum has been held within the previous four years.
(4)	The Parliament of Canada shall, before the expiration of the first parliament following the coming into force of this section, enact a measure consistent with it to provide a reasonable procedure for the orderly administration of referendums to be held pursuant to this section."
2. This amendment may be cited as the Constitution Amendment, 1987.
I read the motion so that the people of Canada will be cognizant of the fact that we need a referendum.
Why do we need a referendum? At the present time there is no federal enabling legislation for Canadians to initiate a vote on public policy or law. The closest example of direct federal legislation is the Canada Elections Act, which governs the election of Members of Parliament. Nevertheless, it is not a law of general application as the public has no mechanism to invoke its application. This means that once Members are elected they cannot be revoked even if they vote against the wishes of their constituents.
My motion before the House is to consider an advance of the referendum process in Canada. The referendum process is created to enhance a direct democracy. It means the participation of constituents in the legislative process. A federal referendum process will enable electors of Canada to become more directly involved in the legislative process.
The particular advantage of the referendum is that it permits the severance of a specific issue of national importance from political party philosophies and enables the public to determine the value of specific national objectives.
Referendums can become a democratic tool to encourage greater public input and control over national objectives by individuals. Presently Canadians are frustrated by public policy being influenced by unelected Senators and appointed judges. More and more Senators and judges are creating legislative policy in Canada rather than interpreting existing legislation.
Conversely the referendum process establishes a method of presenting or referring important legislative issues to a direct public vote of the whole society. The results of a referendum would bind the federal Government to enact legislation to reflect the public will.
There are precedents for this in other countries. For instance, Switzerland enacted in 1848 a referendum process whereby 50,000 signatures can direct the Government to have a referendum on a specific issue. Switzerland is one of the best
direct democracies in the world. It has a system that enables public input on different issues. For instance, recently we had a vote on capital punishment but the public had no input whatsoever. Therefore, it is extremely important that the public be consulted continuously.
In Switzerland, which has these types of referendums, 50,000 signatures can demand a referendum. Even if the upper and lower House have voted on a Bill, that Bill remains not proclaimed for three months. If the 50,000 signatures demand it, the Bill is put to the whole country. It happened quite frequently in Switzerland, that even though both Houses voted on a certain Bill, the Bill did not pass the test of direct democracy.
In Canada, as we know, we have representatives of the people, Members of the House of Commons. But we have as well the non-elected Senate appointed by the Prime Minister of the day. Those Senators are not accountable to anyone but themselves.
We should get rid of them.

As the Hon. Member says, we should vote for a referendum so we can get rid of those Senators or have Senators who are elected. In western Canada, we believe that it is essential to have a Triple E Senate, an elected, effective and equal Senate. This would have brought more democracy to our Confederation. But as the House knows, with the Meech Lake Accord, it will be extremely difficult to bring about an equal, elected and effective Senate because we have created with the Meech Lake Accord a third government institution, the conference of First Ministers. I would say that those are the 11 backroom boys who are going to determine the fate of Canada. It certainly is not a democratic process. We are moving away from direct democracy, a representative democracy, to a Government of 11 First Ministers. Recently, they have determined we should have free trade. On this issue all but two or three First Ministers were in agreement. But a question of national importance should be put directly to the people of Canada. Referendums create a democratic forum where the public will be involved. Federal general elections do not represent single issues of policy and law. Referendums will not be greatly influenced by personalities and political loyalties.
It has become apparent to many Canadians that Parliament is no longer the sole forum of Canadian political policy formation. Our constitutional system of Government has reduced the control and input of individual Canadians in the federal Government. The growth of the Constitution and its Parliamentary rule in Canada has weakened the traditional role and contribution of individual Members of Parliament. The growth of the constitutional rights and laws have created corresponding powers for the courts.
In the past five years we have witnessed unelected judges not only interpreting laws but in fact creating new federal policies
April 14, 1988

based upon their interpretation of Canadian society. We have permitted a constitutional democracy to develop whereby the policies of a duly elected Government of Canadians can be declared unacceptable by five appointed judges who are not directly accountable to Canadians. As I said previously, the Meech Lake Accord has further reduced the public's representative role in Canadian policy development. An unelected Senate will remain enshrined in the Constitution with appointment powers delegated to the provincial Premiers.
A referendum process will enable Canadians to directly introduce policies of national importance to rectify such judicial powers. Judges employ the interpretation of laws based upon their personal interpretation of Canadian values and morals. The recent Supreme Court Morgentaler decision is a clear example of a constitutional system enabling judges to set social standards upon Canadians. Referendums will be an effective mechanism for categorizing and articulating the popular will of Canadians directly into the parliamentary process. Referendums would also enable the consistent protection of Canadian public policy as changes in elected Government often leaves important social issues exposed to change by bureaucrats.
The federal civil service has become the permanent Government of Canada, always present to protect its role and status in policy development. It has become clear to Canadians that upper echelon civil servants, the mandarins, control exceptional power in our public policy domain. Many mandarins possess greater access to cabinet Ministers than do the duly elected Members who compose the accountable Government of Canada. Referendums could act as a control mechanism to provide the Canadian public greater accountability from the permanent Government of Canada and its accountable mandarins.
Referendums are a concept that has been advocated by advocates of direct democracy. This is what we want, direct democracy. People should be able to express their will upon the Government. I think this is a fundamental principle of democracy. I hope that Members of this House will allow this motion to be voted upon because if they do not, I think at that point they do not believe in direct democracy.
We have created in Canada a monster. I would call it a monster of governments. We have the unelected Senate which does not represent the will of the people. As we have seen recently, it is refusing to pass a Bill on immigration that is so important to Canadians. If Meech Lake is accepted, it will contain a unanimity clause which will prevent us from getting rid of this institution that prevents Canadians from having input into their legislation.
It is proposed that a referendum on any matter within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal Parliament could be initiated by proclamation of the Government of Canada or by a petition of not less than 20 per cent of the electors of
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Canada. I use the figure 20 per cent. In Switzerland, they use the figure of 3 per cent but we must have safeguards and I accept the figure of 20 per cent. Those electors address their petition to the House of Commons, thereby petitioning for a referendum addressing an issue of national importance as determined by the electors of Canada.
I would hope that once this motion passes, the provincial Governments and municipalities would as well accept a referendum process. Such a process exists in Switzerland where there is a referendum process at the national level, at the canton level which corresponds to our provincial level and at the municipal level. The process is binding on those Governments.
Issues of monetary policy of national interest, whether it is abortion or capital punishment, should be voted upon directly by the people if the people feel that their representatives have not brought forward a Bill in accordance with the wishes of the majority of Canadians. As I said, I hope that Members across who believe in direct democracy will not talk out this motion. I hope they will be faithful to their electors and will permit the motion to be voted upon.
I see Members from the New Democratic Party and from the Liberal Party here. I am sure they believe in democracy. Therefore, I would ask them to let this motion be voted upon.

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear part of the argument presented by the Hon. Member in defence of his motion. I think he will find that it is not likely to be deemed altogether defensible on both sides of the House. His problem is not that Members on this side will keep it from coming to a vote. The probability is that Members on all sides would defeat it on the basis of what they know to be the parliamentary system.
I would like to discuss this motion in the context of the experience to which I am privy as the Member from Windsor-Walkerville, a riding which is close to the American border. I will refer to a few examples of what he has suggested be done and will indicate what the dangers are if what he proposes were to be done. Of course, we understand that the Hon. Member's philosophical bent would not necessarily reject the situations that have arisen as a consequence of the acceptance of his proposition in the states of the United States at least.
During the course of the Hon. Member's intervention, he indicated, as an example of his complete misapprehension of what the democratic process is all about under a parliamentary system, that during the debate on capital punishment, the people were not allowed to be heard. If it were not unparliamentary to say so, I would say that that was a flat-out lie, but I cannot say that it is a flat-out lie. All I can say is that it certainly was not the truth.
The fact is that the people were heard. They were heard extensively. I for one, and I am sure most Members of the House as well, considered very carefully the views of those who

April 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
expressed themselves as they did to a very extensive degree on the question of capital punishment. We reached a conclusion based, we think, on well informed opinion and a strong sense of responsibility.
I do not want to be trite by quoting the historical references with respect to the duties of Members of Parliament to be advised by their own intellect and their own knowledge and to strain in so much as possible to make decisions on behalf of those who elect them on the basis of good, solid information and careful thought. Nevertheless, I will remind the Hon. Member, as most of us have been reminded repeatedly, that there is a view of this Elouse which imposes upon us that responsibility. To suggest for a moment that it is a contradiction of democracy to state quite clearly that there are issues so complex as not to be easily subject to a referendum method does not follow that view.
Let us look at some of the consequences of the Hon. Member's particular point of view in the State of Michigan, for example. In the State of Michigan, as in so many other states of the United States, there is the most horrible kind of poverty in large urban areas. This occurs in states which have referenda. Why is this? It is because those referenda have allowed the taxpayers to make decisions about when the taxpayers will or will not, for example, pay taxes and whether or not taxes will be paid.
It would take some kind of empty-headed thinking process to believe that the responsibility we have to raise taxes from time to time would be given a favourable response from most taxpayers. In the United States, the consequences of this have been clear. The majority have seen that the black minority in Detroit, for example, is without satisfactory schools. A situation has been created where there is no chance of that being corrected. The Hon. Member would have the majority make every decision without limitation and without assuring a process of careful deliberation of all the factors involved in any decision.
We have a responsibility here which I consider to be a very important one and at times a very trying one. It may be the Hon. Member's bent to avoid the necessity of making decisions, but I for one, and I am sure other Members of the House as well, recognize that the democratic process is not one which is satisfied by collecting signatures on referenda or petitions. It is a question of the electorate choosing those who will represent them best, not because they always reflect the majority opinion but because they are equally able to defend the rights of minorities and, much more important, because they are willing to give the study to any issue that is necessary to reach a decision that will be in the interests of all the people, without conceding to a method which, on the basis of our experiences with petitions, would lead to a fallacious image of democracy and in fact to its utter failure. Therefore, if this motion comes to a vote, I will vote against it. I would support the Hon. Member on only one thing. Let us have the vote and let us reject the proposition.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to take part in this afternoon's debate. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy), is asking us to consider an amendment to the Constitution entitled the Constitution Amendment, 1987. This amendment would allow for referenda to be initiated on any matter coming within the purview of Section 91 of the Constitution Act, 1867, by proclamation of the Government of Canada or by petition of not less than 20 per cent of the electors of Canada.
I would like to begin my comments by reminding Hon. Members of another constitutional amendment, the 1987 Constitutional Accord. On October 23, 1987, by an overwhelming majority of 246 to 16 votes, and with the support of all three Party Leaders, this House approved the 1987 Accord which truly marks a turning point in our constitutional history. The Accord closes the difficult chapter that began when Quebec was left out of the agreement leading to patriation and to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in 1982.
The 1982 reform was a major advance. Besides patriation, it included constitutional recognition of equality and other fundamental rights of our multicultural heritage, aboriginal rights, the rights of official language minorities and our regional strengths.
However, the 1982 Agreement was incomplete: It did not include Quebec. Quebec's return to the constitutional fold is the signal achievement of the 1987 Accord. To bring Quebec fully into the constitutional fold, to strengthen and reaffirm the partnership of Confederation, and to establish a framework for building the partnership of tomorrow are proud achievements, and ones which strengthen the fabric of Confederation as a whole.
Quebec was, of course, legally bound by the Constitution Act, 1982, but it rejected the legitimacy of the new Act, including the Charter, and subsequently announced its intention not to participate in the constitutional process until its constitutional concerns had been addressed.
This was damaging for Canada in two respects. Quebec's isolation made constitutional amendments more difficult to achieve, as we witnessed in our discussions on aboriginal constitutional issues. However, more importantly, Quebec's continued isolation ran the risk of festering and creating a very serious problem for another generation to resolve, perhaps in less tranquil times. That is why it was such a joyous occasion when First Ministers reached unanimous agreement on an Accord which satisfies Quebec's aspirations within Canada and allows Quebec to embrace voluntarily and completely the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
A major reason for the success of the Quebec round of negotiations was the agreement by all Governments to deal with the Quebec issue as a constitutional priority and to defer discussions on other constitutional issues. This distinction
April 14, 1988

between the Quebec round and a second round of constitutional negotiations effectively prevented linkage and was key to the Meech Lake success. With great respect to my colleague, the Member from Calgary East we must not lose sight of that objective by entertaining further amendments to the Constitution of Canada, however commendable those proposals may be, before the Accord is ratified by all provincial legislative assemblies.
The place to deal with further constitutional progress is in the second round. The Accord itself guarantees a forum for further constitutional talks at annual conferences of First Ministers. In particular, the Accord requires the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to convene a First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution at least once a year. Agenda items will include Senate reform, roles and responsibilities in relation to fisheries, and such other matters as may be agreed upon.
Before I sit down, I would like to reflect briefly on the role of public participation in the constitutional process and in particular with regard to the 1987 Accord.
The Accord was forged in the democratic tradition of our country. The issues it resolves have been debated for years in past constitutional negotiations, by the media, by scholars, and by interested Canadians. First Ministers scrupulously respected and surpassed the procedures laid down in the 1982 amending formula.
The hearings of the Special Joint Committee on the Accord ensured that the terms of the Accord were well communicated to the people of Canada and that it was carefully scrutinized. During four weeks of intensive hearings, the joint committee elicited 246 briefs and communications, and heard testimony from more than 80 individuals or groups. The joint committee concluded the Accord represents a reasonable and workable package of constitutional reforms and recommended its adoption by Parliament.
I might point out that the hearings of the joint committee were the first of their kind to have been held on a specific constitutional amendment. The timetable of the hearings was a demanding one, and one which required all involved to focus their energies and attention on the task at hand. While recognizing the magnitude of their task, the committee concluded their schedule was not an unrealistic one or one which excluded meaningful public participation. As the committee put it, "The process has provided us with a strong basis upon which to evaluate the 1987 Accord." The committee also noted that "any fundamental flaws in the Accord would have emerged in the course of this process." However, it is clear that we as parliamentarians, and our opposite numbers in provincial legislatures, could do more, and I welcome the joint committee's recommendations for an expanded parliamentary role through the committee process in giving expert and interested Canadians a voice in proposing the agenda items for First Ministers and in exploring issues First Ministers have agreed to address.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
I do not think anyone can realistically quarrel with the joint committee's conclusion that "a conference of First Ministers will likely always be necessary as the final step to reach agreement on proposed constitutional amendments." Nor, however, can we quarrel with the committee's observation that flexibility after First Ministers have made a decision will always be limited.
In this regard, I note the committee's recommendation that, together with the other place, we create a standing joint committee on constitutional reform, to, as the committee recommends, put "the emphasis on a more open process before First Ministers meet to discuss constitutional issues." I think this is an interesting idea and one which merits further consideration. Indeed, it seems to me that a committee process might provide an ideal forum to examine proposals such as the one we have before us today. Public hearings could be held where Canadians, experts and interested individuals and groups, could make known their concerns and contribute their ideas into the process. Through such processes, Canadians could have a real influence on the course of constitutional reform.
In the meantime, let us not forget that our immediate task is to do everything in our power to ensure the Accord is adopted as quickly as possible, so that the second round can begin on a sound basis, with Quebec's full participation.
I am pleased to note that, in addition to this House, the Accord has been ratified by the legislative assemblies of Quebec, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and debate on the resolution is well under way in Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and Prince Edward Island. The Ontario Select Committee has nearly completed its hearings, and I understand from media reports that debate has begun in British Columbia.
It is heartening to see that the momentum generated by First Ministers on June 3, 1987, continues. For the Constitutional Accord of 1987 is not an ending. It is a beginning. It will set the constitutional reform process on the road again.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity, before this numerous audience, to speak to the motion of the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy) in which he proposes to amend the Constitution of Canada by introducing the referendum concept. The Hon. Member would have us include this concept in the Constitution of Canada because he sees this process as absolutely essential to our democratic system. This means that we would put what he calls questions of national interest to a direct vote by all citizens of Canada.
Referendums and direct democracy are not exactly new. In fact, the very concept of democracy, of demos kratos, the strength of the people, apparently originated in Greece, and more precisely in Athens, many centuries ago. At the time, when Athens, like all other cities, was actually a City State, all citizens would be called on when decisions had to be made.

April 14, 1988
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Whenever a decision had to be made on politics, on the polis- the city-on the city's administration, everyone was called to a meeting and a direct, democratic vote was taken.
However, as the city's territory grew, its population realized that direct democracy created certain problems. People were constantly being asked to come and vote on any number of questions related to the city's administration. The farmer in his field and soldiers in their barracks had to drop everything to come and vote. So people said: Direct democracy is all very well, but it might be better to elect a few people to represent us and save us the trouble of going back and forth all the time. This led to an initial form, which developed over time, of a parliamentary system with elected representatives. People chose certain other people to represent them and to speak on their behalf.
That is how a government administered directly by the people changed, over time, and not without great difficulty, into a parliamentary system in which the people elect a number of representatives. In other words, we have people who become part of the government and who defend the general and more specific interests of the people they represent.
Obviously, people opted for a functional rather than an ideal government. And I think the very concept of a referendum is probably the "tentatively" ideal government, provided that referendums are held often. However, we must not forget that a referendum is a kind of snapshot of public opinion at a given time on a given question. These images change over time. Opinions change. The ideals, customs and morality of one era are gone in the next.
The referendum concept, idealistic though it may be, is not without problems. For instance, how are we to define what the Hon. Member refers to in his amendment as national interest? Of course, we cannot have referendums at the drop of a hat, but are we not about to deny the importance of our parliamentary system? If we go back to direct democracy, we are saying, to a certain extent, that the people who represent us today are not doing their job, do not represent public opinion and do not stand up for the fundamental interests of the citizens of this country.
The changing nature of public opinion is one problem. And what about the protection of minority groups? Referendums can be fatal to minorities.
In his proposal, the Hon. Member suggests that 20 per cent of Canadian citizens would be sufficient justification for applying the referendum formula. It sounds like a lot. This is nearly three million people. But consider the city of Toronto. It would be relatively easy to get three million people to support an emotional issue of so-called national interest.
In that case, what about Prince Edward Island? What about Newfoundland? What about the minorities in the Northwest Territories? What about the Yukon? What about francophone
or, in some cases, anglophone minority groups? What would happen to our aboriginal communities?
You know, in a referendum, what with the emotion and public pressure, some rather startling events widely broadcast on television can make public opinion swing and waver; it does not take so long. We saw a striking example of that recently with the refugee issue. A child crying on television has much more impact than a minister's speech. However, with the rather massive arrival of people from abroad, Canadians might say no to any further immigration, if asked in a referendum. It might come down to such a referendum.
And you know what happened in the United States, in California, with Proposition 13 where Californians said they were fed up with taxes. So they put it to a referendum. It was decided that there would be no more tax increases.
At first, that seemed like a bright idea, a good thing to do. It is true that we are burdened by taxes; everyone is fed up with them. Of course the referendum carried by an overwhelming majority, but what have the consequences of this famous Proposition 13 been? It has deprived the government of some $100 billion since 1978. Everyone will say, "Great! Way to go! They got $100 billion less-that money would have come from us. Wonderful!" But what have the consequences been? The highway system is deteriorating. All kinds of municipal and government facilities are running down because of a referendum, a snapshot of public opinion reflecting a temporary fashion, what almost amounted to collective vengeance, because of too many tax increases too close together, perhaps, but now Californians are paying the price. It is the same individuals and communities who are paying for it. Everything is deteriorating, compared to other surrounding states or municipalities that may have undergone tax increases, but at least have quality services.
So there are dangers in going the referendum route. Of course, compared to a constitutional document, for example, a referendum seems to be supported by the whole country. Let us have Canada's Constitution ratified by the whole population. I, for one, would have liked the BNA Act to have been endorsed by a strong majority, and by that I mean most of the citizens. We would have been on much firmer ground had the Constitution Act of 1982 been the subject of a referendum with a very strong majority in favour of it. But what happens when a referendum is won by something like 50.1 per cent or lost by 49.4 per cent? You will find yourselves in situations leading to the kind of divisions which leave no room for change or negotiation.
So, Mr. Speaker, imagine the people being asked directly to consider a Bill of some 350 pages, 12 paragraphs, 14 subsections, printed as big as this.
Fifteen appendices!

And 15 appendices, says my colleague. It will be impossible, I admit, you can see for yourself, Mr. Speaker, you will readily admit it in spite of your great intelligence, we
April 14, 1988

have a hard time figuring out what is what. So think of the ordinary man who is given an 18-inch thick document and told to make up his mind. Are you for or against? Even we are lost. What a mess, Mr. Speaker, you know that, we have to work full time at it just to be able to single out the positive elements of national interest-when there are any, which does not happen very often.
So there is danger in these referendums which may indeed put us in a straitjacket from which escape does not come easily. The advantage of the parliamentary system is that we can be thrown out every four years or so, we can propose new policies or seek re-election. Like you, Mr. Speaker, I hope we will be able to keep up the good work. But if we have to revert to direct democracy in every instance, then we have problems.
There is an other aspect to the question. The laws, as we know, are often ahead of or lag behind public opinion. There may be some pieces of legislation in Canada that are some years ahead of public attitudes, but, Mr. Speaker, some others are reactionary and need to be adapted to take into account the will of the people. But could we accept a decision based on an occasional and dangerous snapshot of opinion polls? I find it hard to live with that but despite all the shortcomings of our system, despite the theoretical and almost romantic appeal of direct democracy, I would not put such a proposition in the Constitution, at least in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is our role to represent this country and our constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased in turn to take a few minutes of the House to express my views on the motion just tabled by the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy). In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague for Calgary East for the work he put into the preparation of his motion. I would like to add that for a major part of his presentation, Mr. Speaker, I can but agree with him on that part, certainly, that deals with the Senate's encroachment on elected Members of this House. There are many other things also on which I had to fight alongside the Hon. Member for Calgary East and on which I was in total agreement with him. I also note that a lot of work went into his motion, his bill, a lot of research coming from a man of absolute integrity and a very able Member.
As to the actual contents of his motion, Mr. Speaker, this is another story, and I cannot agree with the motion as such. He constantly refers to democracy, direct democracy. Mr. Speaker, each election is an exercise in democracy. That is a democratic process, direct democracy needless to say.
I feel that Canadians are rather bored with being called upon to vote so often. They often told me: We elected a Government, we elected a Member, let him do his job afterwards. If we have to give our views each time the Government has a decision to make, we have other things to look after. We
Constitution Amendment, 1987
should trust our elected representatives, that is what we elected them for.
If each time the Government wants to make a decision, everyone had to go out and vote, there would be no end to that, and there would be no need for the House of Commons, with its Speaker, for a Prime Minister, etc., if on every major decision we went through direct democracy. As you know, Mr. Speaker, major questions are like an accordion. Some might say for instance that what is significant is the budget, or capital punishment; it could be abortion, it could be a million matters. And each individual would have his or her own priorities. Will these matters be put directly to voters each time, in order to know what is the significant issue? Would that not lead to chaos? In my view, it would also be a loss of time, it would be disturbing our fellow citizens in an absolutely needless way, not to mention the costs. As we know, a referendum is very expensive, just as elections are, and Canadians have other things to do than spend money for absolutely no reason and also be disturbed at every moment.
Some colleagues referred to the process in Switzerland. Apparently this would be the country in which there is the greatest number of referendums. Even in that country, Mr. Speaker, the credibility of that referendum process is declining. Initially, it would seem that from 60 to 65 per cent of citizens used it, went to vote. But currently the percentage has sunk below 40 per cent. So if the Swiss could be called the fathers of referendums, they themselves do not believe in it anymore.
My colleague for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy) also referred to the vote we had a few weeks ago, or rather a few months, concerning capital punishment. But on that I think he overlooked one essential aspect. What did he forget? Something I am sure he, like most of my colleagues, did: before voting in the House, he made an effort to find out what the people thought. And since it was a free vote, I should now congratulate our Prime Minister for having allowed us to hold a free vote on an extremely important and controversial issue. I did it myself: I consulted my constituents before voting. Of course, I am not here to represent myself or to defend some personal idea but to represent my constituents' ideas. So when the issue is extremely important in my view, as capital punishment was in the past and other issues will be in the future-I am thinking about abortion legislation, etc.-we should ask Canadians what they think. This kind of consultation would be much less costly than a referendum and make it possible for us to find out just what our constituents think.
You know that when only 20 or 25 per cent of the people respond through a referendum they do not necessarily represent the interests and the will of the whole population.
We have excellent tools at our disposal to be able to consult the people, such as parliamentary bulletins, and we can send householders four times a year. I should think that is enough. We can consult people four times a year on what we feel are major issues, and it does not cost us a cent. I do that all the

April 14, 1988
Adjournment Debate
time and I urge my colleagues to do the same thing. If we really believe in democracy, which consists in representing the views of our constituents as eloquently and faithfully as we can, that is an essential tool to ask them what they think. We could always include a removable page which they can return to us. A constituent does not have to change his routine, he does not have to leave work to go and vote, yet at the same time he can tell us what he thinks. In a case like that they just send us the removable page and tell us their views, and after that the parliamentarians or the Members should act accordingly.
To me that kind of democracy is much more direct than .. . [English]

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the adjournment motion to refer to a question which I put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on April 12 last as recorded on page 14 387 of Hansard. I do so because I think that the Prime Minister erred in his answer and I should like to bring a correction to Hansard and stick with the facts.
I put a question to the Prime Minister about conditions in Saskatchewan and pointed out that the Government has introduced and is discussing Bill 2 which according to many is a step backward and will restrict considerably language legislation confirmed on February 25 last under a decision delivered by the Supreme Court.
It will be remembered that the Supreme Court had pronounced judgment in the case of Saskatchewan and perhaps also with respect to Alberta because both provinces were carved within the same territory; it decided that section 110 of the legislation creating the provinces had been copied as it were from the same legislation concerning the Northwest Territories ... therefore clause 110 directed the Government to allow English and French in the legislature and in the courts.
The Supreme Court rendered its judgment and gave the government two options, as we all know. The first option: You can declare you are unilingual by adopting legislation that says all statutes enacted since 1905 are valid. The second option: Instead of saying you are unilingual, you could have your statutes translated and negotiate appropriate arrangements with the official language minority group.
I put the question to the Prime Minister to establish that many premiers, Mr. Bourassa as well as Mr. Getty and Mr. Devine, are using the language question in Saskatchewan for their own political and provincial purposes. I am sorry I have to say this, but I think it is high time these premiers took action and stopped making promises or the kind of unacceptable statements made by Mr. Bourassa who said, substantially, and I am quoting from an article that appeared in La Presse on April 12: "I wouldn't want other governments to interefere with the way we treat our Anglophone minority in Quebec, and so I respect the way the province is treating its Francophone minority".
I could quote many more instances, Mr. Speaker. The papers are full of them. Mr. Getty said he would proceed like Saskatchewan did but that in any event, Alberta would take care of its own business. Mr. Devine tells us that in ten or fifteen years the province of Saskatchewan will be bilingual. No kidding!
The majority of the population of Saskatchewan is anglophone. We know that. The Province has statutes, and under those statutes, it had certain statutory obligations. There was one obligation that had not been met, through no fault of the Saskatchewan Francophones who, until recently with Father Mercure, lacked the money and the legal arguments to go before the courts and stand up for their rights.
Hon. Members will recall that Manitobans were given back their language rights when George Forest, in 1974-75-76, decided to go before the courts to stand up for his rights in Manitoba. Finally, in 1979, he won his case.
However, my main point today is the point I was trying to make to the Prime Minister, namely that asking Francophone communities to put their faith in Mr. Devine's statements would, in my view, be asking too much of this minority which today has yet to receive from the Saskatchewan Government the most basic, the most essential services as far as education is concerned. In fact, the courts have been asked to decide whether Section 23 of the Constitution Act of 1982 gives Francophones in this province the right to have their own autonomous school boards.
He should not go too far in his suggestion that there is much good will on the part of the Government.
In his reply, the Prime Minister said:
If I am not mistaken, Mr. Speaker,-
-I am quoting him verbatim-
April 14, 1988

-the report of the Commissioner for Official Languages indicates that in recent years there has been substantial progress in Saskatchewan with respect to the use of French.
I perused the report of the Commissioner for Official Languages which I had read before and tried to find the comment which could have given the Prime Minister this idea and suggest that in recent years there had been substantial progress in Saskatchewan with respect to the use of French. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is no mention of that in this report; on the contrary, and I should like to quote a statement made by the Commissioner for Official Languages on page 159, and I quote;
Their relative weight no doubt accounts for some of the special difficulties they-
-the Fransaskois-
. . . face and for the sharp debates which sometimes surround the issue of official bilingualism in the West.
-I continue-
-the year-
-this is 1987-
-witnessed a number of unfortunate confrontations over demands for French language schools, legal battles over the right of accused persons to trials in the official language of their choice and controversy surrounding the status and use of French in provincial legislatures.
I was quoting the Commissioner for Official Languages. What he said is entirely different from what the Prime Minister stated in the House in his reply on April 12 when he said that there had been substantial progress. He should not try to ... I am not saying that he tried intentionally to mislead me, but the Prime Minister should state openly that there are serious problems in western Canada. These are serious problems which must be dealt with. We are going to solve them if we deal seriously with western Canadians and declare outright that the rights of minorities should be respected wherever they are, whether in Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba or Ontario, in short, all Canadian provinces, including Quebec. They have a right to survive in Canada and I hope that the Prime Minister whom I know very well will make sure from now on-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member must realize that there have been many Commissionner reports and many words in this one, but this is not the gist of the issue. I am sure the Hon. Member realizes that the Prime Minister has already been questioned at length on the issue of language rights in Saskatchewan. He clearly explained his own and the Government's position on this issue.
The Prime Minister also recalled his own and the Government's commitment to promote the full recognition and the use of French and English in Canadian society. But there is a
Adjournment Debate
difference between the parties in this House, a difference of attitude. We, the Conservatives, believe that discussion and cooperation have more to offer than confrontation. But the Liberals and the NDP believe that confrontation is better than co-operation and discussion.

There is a big difference on a very important and fundamental issue in this country, the issue of language. I do not think the nation is well served by any political tactic that attempts to heighten divisions. It is surely an issue in this country, and I commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for the degree to which he provides that co-operation and discussion of leadership on this very important and essential issue to the fabric of our nation.

I urge the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) to study the issue in the same non-partisan spirit that he demonstrated when previously taking stands; he will recognize, as did the NDP leader, that the Prime Minister is making positive and constructive efforts in that matter.
He is meeting today in the Province of Saskatchewan. He has offered the House his willingness to report fully and completely on those discussions.
I simply say to the Hon. Member opposite: "Be non-partisan on this issue, invite the Prime Minister to report to the House". Surely co-operation and discussion is the way to advance national unity on the language issue.
IMMIGRATION-QUERY WHETHER MINISTER HAS CONSULTED CANADIAN BAR AND THE SENATE/ REQUEST FOR 60-DAY DELAY ON DEPORTATIONS

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have a chance to speak on a question that I raised two weeks ago. The question concerned the problem or collection of problems that our country has in connection with the backlog of refugee claimants and the need for new legislation on refugee determination.
The legislation has been stalled by a number of causes, which I will not take time to go into now because I have discussed them before, and the backlog has been increased by the allowing of various national groups to enter through a loophole without imposing a visa restriction as early as could have been done. Also there have been no convictions yet of any of the operators of those scams and no legislation yet to provide the means for better regulating those operators, or no proposal for legislation.
However, the problem is with us. Two weeks ago I asked the then Minister to consider the need for consulting to resolve a practical problem. I asked him if he would consider a package as follows: (1) a 60-day delay on deportation, that is of

April 14, 1988
Adjournment Debate
backlog members, to allow time for consultation; (2) consultation with the Canadian Bar Association and the Senate to make Bill C-55 workable under our existing Constitution and Supreme Court; and (3) creation of a new administrative review that fairly identifies the people who are effectively established in Canada, taking into account help from their relatives and their work record.
I want to take up each of those points in order. The 60-day freeze is an arbitrary number that I picked, two months, to give time for consultation. I agree with the words that I heard from across the way, from the speaker for the Government, that there are times when confrontation is not wanted. I think this is a time when consultation could be appropriate.
At present the Turks are being deported, although Canadians where they are living have said that they want them to stay. Obviously there are many others of the 48,000 who will come into question in the very near future and farther. Many people doubt that this Government will in fact deport 48,000 people during this year. The number might be greater, or it might be smaller, but it is in the tens of thousands.
The suggestion therefore is, rather than deporting a few and then perhaps working out a plan that would have treated them differently had it been in operation earlier, that we hold in order to treat all in the same way. During that two-month hold we could do two major things. There could be consultation on Bill C-55. Granted there has been a lot of talk on it so far, but the main point on which we should consult is to bring it into line with the Supreme Court decision given three years ago which says that everybody who comes here-that is, if he claims refugee status and if he is in Canada-has a right to have his or her claim fully heard by the people who will decide on the merits of the claim. That is denied to most people by Bill C-55. Furthermore, what we have for those people who do go to have their claims heard is a double process, two hearings instead of one. If we could get rid of that screening, in accordance with the advice of the Bar Association and all the lawyers in private practice who have discussed this with anyone I know of, we would do two things; we would speed up the process of Bill B-55 itself, which we all agree is desirable, and we would be bringing it into line with the Supreme Court decision on the meaning of our Constitution.
If we do not do that, what we have is a Bill that is unworkable. Even if it were declared today, it would be found to be unworkable. We have that on the advice of all the lawyers who are not being hired by the Government to support it. That is part of the reason for its delay.
The second thing that could be done would be to work out fairer plans for a new administrative review, to review the backlog of refugee claimants on an individual basis to find out who is or who is about to be adequately settled. The Government has already done that with tens of thousands of people. The Minister issues tens of thousands of permits every year.
There is nothing extraordinary and certainly nothing illegal about this procedure. It would not be hurting the regular immigrants because the Government last year, according to its figures, brought in 9,000 more than it had planned to bring in. So for the ones who were brought in in the administrative review last year, it did not block them.
It should be made more fair than the last administrative review. It should take account of the people who are receiving genuine help from their families in getting settled. It should take account, for example, of a Guyanese woman who is earning $13,000 a year in a factory. That does not come up to our Stats Canada standards, but she is in fact supporting her two children. She has done that for several years. That should be recognized. She, like many Canadian born people, is paid less than what we consider an acceptable wage but she is surviving. She is working and looking after her family. She should not be turfed out because she does not come up to an abstract wage standard.
Likewise, people in areas of high unemployment should not be penalized because they are in areas of high unemployment. Therefore, I am hoping the Government will consider a package like this which would benefit the Government, the refugees and the country by resolving this impasse.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member and I have served for some considerable period of time on inquiries into immigration. In many ways we have similar attitudes about many kinds of solutions. However, I think the Member is off base in several ways. He starts his discourse today by he saying he cares about the operators of scams and the fact that none have yet been convicted, but there is a problem in the current law in getting evidence and convicting. Then the Member says that nothing is on the table that would change that situation. Bill C-84 is on the table. It has very clear-cut provisions designed to stop that kind of scam, to get convictions, and to stop the assault on Canada's immigration borders. I think the Hon. Member knows that. I am not quite sure why he said what he said.
There is an argument on the constitutionality of some of the provisions in Bill C-84 and Bill C-55. These two pieces of legislation were dealt with by this House on an emergency basis last summer. They were stalled in the Senate month after month after month.
My experience goes back to June of 1985 when we got into a real clear understanding of the refugee situation. We were dealing in this Chamber with a piece of legislation designed to increase the strength of the number of people in the Immigration Appeal Board so they could deal with the reunification of family members, the real immigration side, and the assault on refugee claims by bogus claimants. We were delayed by the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party. We have had this since June of 1985. Every time the Government tries to do something positive to straighten out the situation, to clear up the difference between bogus claimants and real refugees, to
April 14, 1988

really help refugees and to help the family reunification process, we get delays.
What is the Hon. Member asking us to do? The very first thing out of the box in his original question and again today, is a 60-day delay. Well 60 days more delay will invite more scams. This Government says no to more scams. Let us get on with it. Let us get the deal back from the Senate, get it in place and start to clear up the mess.

subtopic: TAX REFORM-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PAY INTEREST ON INCOME TAX COLLECTED
TAX REFORM-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PAY INTEREST ON INCOME TAX COLLECTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 18, I pointed out to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that the Government had just given itself an interest-free loan of over $1 billion. This is because, under what the Government is pleased to call tax reform, income tax has been reduced for Canadians since January 1, 1988, in some ways, but they will not see this reduction in their pay cheques until July 1988.
I noted as well that the Conservative chairman of the finance committee had been quoted as calling this situation a rip-off. The Minister did not say that he would do the correct thing by paying the interest on this loan back to Canadians. Instead, he responded that this situation exists for various administrative reasons.
I would like to point out again today that this rip-off is just one of many rip-offs imposed by this Government since it came to power. It is just one of others that the Government has tried to keep rather quiet about.
Another silent tax grab is the Government's requirement that employers deduct their income tax, unemployment insurance premiums and Canada Pension Plan contributions and remit them weekly instead of fortnightly. That was increased from once a month in January of 1987. This gives the Government a one-time increase in its cash flow for this year of $1.6 billion.
The Government made another silent tax grab in the 1985 Budget when it deindexed the income tax system. By doing this, the Government has made inflation work for it. Each year since 1985, the rate of increase of benefits such as family allowance has not kept pace with inflation. Neither has the rate at which taxpayers could deduct certain allowances for income tax purposes. This year alone, as a result of deindexation, taxpayers had to pay an extra $750 million to the Government.
I would ask again, when will the Government admit to Canadians that it is at their expense that the smoke-and-mirrors routine that is miscalled tax reform is being carried out?

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: TAX REFORM-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PAY INTEREST ON INCOME TAX COLLECTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to the question posed by the Hon. Member with regard to the
Adjournment Debate
Government paying interest on income tax collected as a result of the tax reform measures, I would offer the following comments.
In June of 1987 when the White Paper on tax reform was tabled in the House, we were aware that we would not introduce the detailed Ways and Means Motion early enough to change the withholding tables for January 1, 1988, given the time necessary for detailed consultation and review by the parliamentary committee. Therefore, it follows that the earliest date for adjustment to the withholding tables could not be before July 1, 1988. Accordingly, the changes were scheduled to take effect with respect to withholdings on salary and wages paid after July 1, 1988.
It would have been difficult to provide for earlier implementation of these measures for the following reasons. The Government's fiscal year runs from April 1 to March 31. Government expenditures for the year to March 31, 1988, have been based in part upon the revenues collected under existing regulations. In addition, the current fiscal framework was one of the fundamental premises upon which the personal tax rate reductions, introduced as part of the tax reform process, were based.
If such an approach had not been adopted, the reduction in tax rates for 1988 may not have been as significant. The legislation has not yet been introduced to the House and there is no authority which would permit the withholding of lesser amounts. In addition, while the draft legislation respecting the tax reform proposals has just been made public, there may be changes made to the legislation as a result of further input from the public and the finance committee.
While most taxpayers will benefit from the lowering of rates through increased take-home pay, some taxpayers may also have an increase in tax liability due to the elimination of certain tax preferences and the restriction of certain other deductions. This situation is no different from any other year in which relieving measures are introduced in the Budget.
While these measures take effect in a particular year, employers will deduct amounts from salary and wages based upon the tax tables issued as of January of that year. The taxpayer will not receive the benefit until he files his return. Interest is paid in the normal course on refunds paid after April 30.
In closing, it is only reasonable that there be a transitional period for the implementation of such major tax revisions and it is commendable that this has been kept to a short period of six months.
